videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 1 -  Improving System
videos.description:
Transforming urgent and emergency care with real-time intelligence in Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin

Faced with growing pressure on urgent and emergency care (UEC) services, Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin Integrated Care Board (STW ICB) developed an innovative UEC Dashboard to deliver near real-time insight across the whole system—from NHS 111 and ambulance services to emergency departments, hospital flow, and community-based care.
What sets this dashboard apart is its integration of NHS England’s Making Data Count methodology, with advanced Statistical Process Control (SPC) charts at its core. These enable frontline teams and system leaders to detect variation, identify trends, and respond quickly to emerging pressures.
The solution is underpinned by an automated SSIS-driven data pipeline and a robust SQL-based data warehouse. Using a star-schema model, data flows securely into Power BI through an On-Premises Gateway for regular, reliable refreshes. Users can interrogate data at multiple time intervals—daily to yearly—tailored to operational needs.
The results have been transformative: faster, smarter decisions; a shared language for performance; and a system-wide shift toward data-driven action. Recognised by NHS England’s Making Data Count national and regional teams as a benchmark model, the dashboard has directly contributed to improved system performance and played a pivotal role in supporting the ICB’s exit from legal oversight.
This project exemplifies how strategic use of data and technology can enhance resilience, promote collaboration, and ultimately improve patient outcomes—demonstrating the power of workplace technology to drive system-wide improvement in the most high-pressure environments.

Craig Lovatt, Senior Business Intelligence Lead (NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wreking)
Kirsty Dyass, Quality Analyst (NHS Shropshire, Telfird and Wrekin)
Craig Kynaston, Head of Business Intelligence and Analytics
(Shropshire Telford and Wrekin ICB)

videos.title: HACA2025- Day 1- Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Building and implementing a patient non- attendance prediction system using commonly available data
"Introduction 

Missed diagnostic endoscopy appointments (“did not attend”, or DNA) negatively affect cancer outcomes by delaying treatment and worsening prognosis. DNAs also waste clinical resources and lengthen waiting times. Based on historical DNA data, we developed a machine learning–based predictive model, allowing for targeted interventions for patients at greater risk of non-attendance. 

Aim, Methods, Results 
Aim: To use PAS (Patient Administrative System) data to identify patients most at risk of not attending their upcoming endoscopy.  High-risk patients are then contacted by a Health Navigator, who can offer targeted support and improve attendance rates. 

Methods: We trained an XGBoost model on 39,447 endoscopy appointments across six hospitals over the course of two years. The model predicted binary outcomes (DNA vs. attendance), optimised for AUROC and calibration error. Key predictors included prior DNAs, socio-economic deprivation (IMD), rurality, age, gender, and procedure type. 

Results: Patients with ≥10% predicted DNA risk were called by healthcare navigators over a 12 week period. Compared with a 17% baseline DNA rate, calling high risk patients reduced DNAs to 5% among contacted patients and 11% overall. Across 650 monitored appointments, 52 DNAs were recorded; scaling suggests ~150 annual DNAs could be prevented. Hence, the calls achieved a ~10% reduction in DNA rates. 

Impact (50 words) 
The project has led to an estimated saving of £37k per year. It also shaped system-level approaches to tackling health inequalities, informing our Trust’s Lifelong Care Strategy and influenced local policy (including prison pathways). Expansion of this approach is underway across five additional services, including a collaboration with Local Authorities. Integration into the booking software Healthcall is planned, embedding predictive analytics into routine practice to improve access and equity. 

Lessons learned 
Predicting patients’ DNA risk is possible using basic data taken from Patient Administrative Systems.  These predictions can be used to perform an intervention with tangible benefits for both patients and hospitals.   

There are diverse reasons for which patients don’t attend their appointments, both personal and systemic, with different strategies to tackle them.  

Richard Bilsborough, Data Scientist/Information Specialist (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust)
Fabian Beigang, Data Scientist / Information Specialist
(Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust)
Chris Wilcockson, Public Health Analyst (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust)

Semi-automated REDCap-R reporting workflow to support scotland's MAT standards

"Monitoring Scotland’s Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) Standards is essential for the National mission on ensuring timely and consistent access to care for people affected by substance use. 
In order to reduce barriers for frontline staff, we developed a semi-automated reporting approach that combines REDCap, a secure data-collection platform, with R flexdashboard and Posit Connect. 
In this talk, we show an example of how the reports and processes were implemented with usability a main priority. The semi-automated design reduces manual handling versus spreadsheet workflows, strengthens information governance, and increases data availability without claiming full automation. The approach is scalable to additional MAT Standards and adaptable to other NHS reporting domains where timely, secure insights are required. 
Analysts refresh an R workflow to generate dashboards that summarise the data in clear graphical formats—such as scatter plots and other visualisations—before securely distributing them to Alcohol and Drug Partnerships (ADPs). By focusing on plots rather than descriptive statistics (e.g., means and medians), the dashboards make it easier for both analysts and non-analysts to quickly identify key information, enabling ADPs to spot gaps and track improvement more effectively. 
This work demonstrates how combining established digital tools (REDCap, R, Posit Connect) with analyst-led refresh can create a sustainable, governance-compliant reporting infrastructure that helps frontline teams act on data, not just collect it"

Manqiu Xiong, Information Analyst (NHS Lothian)

videos.title: HACA 2025- Day 1 - Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Evaluating the impact of Right Care, Right Person
"Right Care, Right Person (RCRP) is being implemented across police forces in England and Wales with the aim of ensuring that vulnerable people get the right support from the right agency. RCRP ensures calls for service relating to mental health are dealt with by the right service, and the police are working in partnership with other agencies to achieve this.

Suffolk Constabulary implemented RCRP from October 2023, starting with calls for service relating to concern for welfare and later including those relating to walk outs from healthcare facilitates and AWOL from mental health establishments, transportation of patients and section 136 Mental Health Act/voluntary mental health patients.

Suffolk Police and the Suffolk & North-East Essex Integrated Care Board commissioned the Suffolk Office of Data & Analytics (SODA) to evaluate the wider implications of RCRP to ensure that members of the public are indeed receiving the ‘right care’. 

Since the launch of RCRP, SODA has collated quarterly data from relevant partners. The data is visualised through a Power BI dashboard, which details how Welfare and Mental Health incidents are dealt with by the police and, if referred under RCRP, where referrals are made. This data is then linked to trends in ambulance call outs, A&E visits and NHS 111 calls, as well as local Specialist Mental Health Services and Suffolk County Council's Children's and Adults Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs. 

Although there were concerns about the impact that RCRP might have on services, we have found that the impact has not been as great as initially feared. We intend to continue to monitor trends to see if this changes.

In November 2025, SODA is scheduled to follow up changes in call/attendance volumes with qualitative research to understand whether these are due to RCRP or if other factors could be behind these changes.

Stephen Parsons, Advanced Analyst C Researcher(Suffolk Office of Data C Analytics)

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 1 - Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Site-level Covid-19 vaccine demand forecasting: Efficiency across NHS vaccination sites

Seasonal COVID-19 vaccination campaigns in England require distributing millions of doses to almost 7,000 sites. The Targeted Deployment Model (TDM) currently manages deployment, balancing site stock levels against expected demand. However, the existing forecasting approach is deterministic and can be inaccurate, leading to over- or under supply, stock wastage, and inefficiencies. Improving forecast accuracy is essential to optimise resource use and support timely delivery.
Aim
To develop a more accurate site-level demand forecasting model, so that automated orders generated by TDM better reflect true local demand.
Methods
We used historical data on vaccination events, bookings, and site characteristics to train and evaluate a multivariate gradient boosting model (LightGBM). Feature engineering was critical to adapt this tree-based method for time series forecasting. Forecasts were produced at site level with a 14-day horizon and evaluated using walk-forward validation to replicate real-world conditions. Models were benchmarked against the existing TDM forecast using MAE, SMAPE, and bias. To capture variation, sites were clustered by demand patterns (e.g. advance bookings vs walk-ins) and activity size, and accuracy assessed across these groups. The forecasting pipeline was designed for scalability to nearly 7,000 sites and for integration into TDM, ensuring outputs could be used directly in deployment decisions.
Results
LightGBM provided the best balance of speed, accuracy, and flexibility, delivering an approximate 20% improvement in accuracy compared to the deterministic base model. That is, forecast performance across sites yielded a mean absolute error of 4.88 vaccinations and a symmetric mean absolute percentage error of 65.6%, with Bias around 25%. Clustering sites by demand behaviour improved interpretability and highlighted where forecasts diverged most from current allocations (e.g. walk-in heavy versus advance-booking sites). Daily retraining was successfully implemented to ensure forecasts remained relevant throughout campaigns.
Impact
This work informed NHS England’s planning for the October 2025 campaign. Improved forecasts were integrated into the TDM pipeline to automate stock orders, and better match supply with demand across thousands of sites.

Liliana Valles, Senior Data Science Manager (NHS England)
Scarlett Kynoch, Data Scientist (NHS England)
Ilyas Ag Sidiyene, (NHS England)

videos.title: HACA2025- Day 1- Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Virtual fracture clinic improves boast compliance, patient outcomes, and delivers cost savings in lower socio-economic areas 
Background: Lower socio-economic regions have higher pressures on emergency services. Virtual services can reduce the demand on secondary care. We aim to assess the effect of virtual fracture clinics (VFC) on compliance with BOAST guidelines, patient reported outcomes and hospital metrics in an inner city setting with higher levels of social deprivation. 

Methods: A closed-loop prospective audit was performed, comparing outcomes from January to December 2024 (pre-VFC) to February to March 2025 (post-VFC). BOAST 72-hour breach rates, discharge rates, did-not-attend (DNA) rates, surgical conversion rates, patient satisfaction, and projected cost savings were assessed.  

Results: New attendances reduced from 45 to 27 per day. On average, 18 patients were assessed each day in VFC, with a discharge rate of 32.3%, saving 155 appointments.  Required face-to-face (F2F) fracture clinic slots were reduced by 40.9%, from 110 pre-VFC to 65 post-VFC. F2F DNA rates reduced from 23.5% (n=863) pre-VFC to 8.3% (n=26) post-VFC, with a 1.2% (n=9) DNA rate for VFC calls. Pre-VFC, 9.8% of surgical and emergency cases were incorrectly triaged to fracture clinic; this reduced to 1.2% post-VFC. 72-hour BOAST fracture clinic guideline breaches decreased from 37.4% (n=2449) to 14.5% (n=70). 84% of patients preferred VFC over waiting in clinic, where wait times were over 90 minutes. Projected annual cost savings from reduced attendances exceeded £100,000.   

Conclusion: VFC markedly improved BOAST compliance, reduced non-urgent fracture clinic attendances and DNA rates. It expedited urgent cases to on-call pathways. There were exceptional operational cost savings. VFC led to consultant-level decision-making at an earlier point of care, preventing harm and redistributing departmental resources to patient benefit. This audit demonstrated VFC to be a successful model despite high levels of deprivation and one of the largest cohorts of non-English-speaking patients in the UK. 

Rania Khan, Foundation Year 2 Doctor
(NHS England)

Modelling renal care from progression to diagnosis 

We don’t have sufficient capacity to meet future needs for renal services. The Strategy Unit, working collaboratively with Midlands Renal Network, have built a hybrid simulation model of renal care from the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) to kidney replacement therapy (KRT). This collection of models projects both demand, the number of patients flowing into KRT for the next 10 years, and capacity, where they’ll be in the system (dialysis type/living with transplant). Additionally, the simulation allows for the evaluation of interventions for patients at all stages of renal care from the impact of new drugs and prevention strategies to direct changes to KRT care pathways. This work is crucial for informing and evidencing future renal plans. Our aim is to role this out nationally over the coming year and open-source our model to improve access and model sustainability.

Lucy Morgan, Analytics Manager (Simulation) (Strategy Unit)
Sally Thompson, Senior Healthcare Analyst (Strategy Unit)

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 1- Improving System Flow
videos.description:
The GP resilience matrix: A strategic tool for targeted primary care support
Primary care resilience is often only recognised at the point of crisis. We set out to make earlier signals visible — so that practices under pressure can be supported sooner, protecting patient access and staff sustainability. The GP Resilience Matrix was first developed in Excel and became a widely used, trusted product. It integrated 40+ indicators across clinical quality (QOF), workforce (FTE per 10k), demand/flow (GPAD; 111/999/UTC/ED per 10k), patient experience (GPPS), and context (IMD, CQC). Standardisation with z-scores enabled fair comparison, and practices were banded from “Higher Achieving” to “Review Identified”. 

While effective, Excel became labour-intensive to maintain and too rigid for live use, creating inefficiencies that affected timeliness. We rebuilt in Power BI; retaining the analytics while improving usability and sustainability. This directly responds to the HACA 2025 theme by showing how analysis can rise to the challenge of shaping future-ready systems. 

Data was structured into a relational model; DAX calculated scores, composites and bands. We used the project to stress-test our “woodyard” BI operating model — data investigation, engineering, development, visualisation — managed through weekly updates and mapping sessions. 

Key user changes included: maps for geographic context, flexible filters, deeper drill-through, curated table exports, and adjustable criteria so thresholds/weights can reflect local priorities. These reduced dependence on analysts and made the tool practical in live PCN and ICB meetings. 

 Demo feedback was strong: users noted it offered more flexibility and insight than national platforms. Locally, colleagues have already used it in DES/S96 support conversations to benchmark and prompt improvement, helping target support upstream in primary care and ensure resources are allocated more equitably. By reducing manual effort and streamlining refresh, the rebuild also improved system flow and reduced wasted effort, freeing analyst time for higher-value work. 

 Analytics only helps if people can work with it; rigour must balance with UX; our schema build could have been more efficient; diverse team perspectives added value; resourcing and stakeholder availability constrained pace. Moving from Excel to Power BI reduced maintenance burden, improving timeliness and sustainability. 

Next steps: publish a documentation package (business rules/user guidance), automate refresh, and validate whether resilience bands predict future stress. 

This evolution shows how analysis can move from a static product to a dynamic, explainable model at the heart of resilience planning for future health systems. 


Ritesh Raj, Population Health C Strategy Lead Analyst
(NHS Kent and Medway ICB)"

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 1-  Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Making easy the default: Driving digital uptake in NHS 111 dental and prescription pathways using Behaviour Change Theory

High call volumes to NHS 111, often from low acuity callers, are straining urgent and emergency care services. Using the EAST  (easy, attractive, social, timely) framework, new messaging was developed and trialled to encourage London patients to use digital services for dental and prescription needs.

The aim was to measurably increase the uptake of digital services, achieving a channel shift for patients from traditional phone-based services to digital pathways.

A randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted to assess the effect of three messaging formats on digital service uptake. Three formats of message content (Easy, Social, Control) were informed by post‑call patient experience survey responses from over 12,000 patients and structured using the EAST behaviour change framework. Patients contacting NHS 111 for dental or prescription queries were randomly assigned to receive each message type. Trends in uptake and the relative performance of each message formats were evaluated using Statistical Process Control (SPC) methods.

A significant, sustained increase in digital uptake was identified, with ‘Easy’ messaging outperforming others. Uptake improved by 7–12% (dental), 8–12% (repeat prescriptions), and 5–8% (emergency medication) versus control, without adverse impact on 24‑hour call‑back rates.

Adoption of the approach is now underway. Estimated uptake suggests more than 18,000 London patients seeking dental or prescription services annually will shift to digital services, equivalent to 285 eight‑hour call handler workdays saved.

Analysis identified many connected factors influencing results that SPC or RCT alone couldn’t fully demonstrate. System dynamics can map these links, test changes, and find tipping points that inform more adaptable decisions alongside regular monitoring.

Efejiro Ashano, Senior Data Analyst (Guys and St. Thomas NHS)
Kate Lambe, (Health Innovation Network South London)
Helen Sheldon, (Health Innovation Network South London)"

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 1- Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Direct and indirect impacts of industrial action on emergency department attendances in England, 2022-2024: A causal mediation analysis with 20 hospitals
"Background
Between December 2022 and July 2024, the English National Health Service saw 27 periods of industrial action over 78 days, involving hospital and ambulance staff. We examine the impacts of industrial action on the Emergency Department (ED).
Methods
This observation study of unplanned attendances at 20 major (Type 1) EDs in England from August 2022 to July 2024, selected sites with high-quality data across emergency, inpatient, and imaging records. Our primary outcome was the patient’s duration in the ED along with indicators of a strike by one or more of the following staff groups at the mid-point of the patient’s ED stay: (1) resident/junior doctors, (2) consultants, (3) both residents and consultants, (4) paramedics, and (5) nurses. Effects were estimated with accelerated failure time, linear and generalised linear regression models with fixed and random effects (hospital level) within a causal mediation analysis.
Results
The average duration of ED attendances reduced on days affected by residents’ strikes [-12.6%, 95% CI -10.4% to -14.8%], consultant strikes [-5.6%, -2.7% to -8.4%], paramedic strikes [-4.5%, -2.0% to -6.8%], but increased when both residents and consultants were on strike simultaneously [+7.2%, +3.8% to +10.7%]. There were no significant changes to ED durations during nurse strikes [-1.7%, -1.5% to 4.7%]. Changes in emergency inpatient occupancy explained a proportion of the change in average ED durations (resident doctor 10.4%, consultants 53.3%, combined doctors 5.4%, and paramedics 14.3%). The impact of strikes on ED attendance volumes was mixed. The net effect of these changes explained 1.5%, 16.8% and 28.8% of the change in average ED durations observed during residents, combined doctor, and paramedic strikes respectively. During the residents’ strikes, patients were more likely to receive treatments in ED [adjusted incident risk ratio 1.013, 1.008 to 1.018], but less likely to be admitted [adjusted odds ratio 0.963, 0.946 to 0.980]. Efforts to meet the 4-hour target intensified during the resident, consultant and combined doctors strike, but reduced during the nurse and paramedic strikes. This explained 2.7%, and 17.1% of the changes in average ED durations observed during the resident and consultant strikes respectively. There were substantial reductions in many forms of planned hospital care during the resident, consultant and combined doctor strikes, but these did not lead to statistically significant changes in ED durations.
Conclusion
The findings suggest that industrial action—particularly during resident doctor and consultant strikes—was associated with reduced ED durations, due in part, to increased emergency bed availability, reduced ED demand, more intensive patient management, and heightened focus on meeting performance targets. However, most reductions during resident doctor strikes could not be fully explained by measurable factors, indicating other unobserved changes in hospital resources, operations or behaviours. Notably, while reductions in planned care activities were substantial, they did not significantly impact ED flow.

Steven Wyatt, Head of Research C Policy (Strategy Unit)"

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 2 - Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Turning insight into action: Using data to improve asthma outcomes in Dorset
"Introduction 
Many people live with asthma as a long-term condition. Up to 2020, data showed that Dorset had higher asthma mortality rates than other areas in the South West. Overuse of Short-Acting Beta Agonists (SABA) is linked to poor outcomes and increased risk of death. Dorset needed a way to better understand and address prescribing patterns contributing to these risks. 

Aim, Methods and Results 

The aim was to use data to identify patterns of SABA overprescribing and support practices in improving asthma care by increasing the use of preventative treatments. 

Dorset Intelligence and Insight Service (DiiS) developed reports highlighting excessive SABA prescribing across Primary Care Networks (PCNs). These insights enabled practices to review prescribing behaviours and identify patients at risk. Some PCNs used this data to audit care plans and promote the use of inhaled corticosteroids, aligning with national asthma management guidelines. 

The granularity of DiiS data, updated daily and available at person level, allowed targeted interventions. Practices could focus on individuals with high SABA use and adjust treatment plans. This proactive approach supported better clinical decision-making and population health management. 

Across Dorset, SABA overuse declined more rapidly than in other Integrated Care Systems (ICSs) in the South West. PCNs that reduced SABA prescribing saw corresponding drops in asthma-related hospital admissions. Mortality rates from asthma also decreased, suggesting improved outcomes linked to data-informed care. 

Impact 

The project influenced prescribing practices and clinical decision-making across Dorset. DiiS insights enabled timely, targeted action, supporting safer asthma management and contributing to reduced admissions and mortality. 

Lessons Learned 

Real-time, granular data is essential for identifying variation, understanding its causes, and driving effective interventions. DiiS enabled clinicians to act quickly, improving care quality and outcomes. This work shows how data and technology can help reduce risk, personalise care, and support strategic priorities in population health. "


Paul Wilding, Dorset Healthcare University NHS Foundation Trust 
William McConnell, Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

videos.title: HACA2025 - Day 2 - Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Predicting the demand for care homes with service user journeys

"Adult Social Care (ASC) provides support to those who find it difficult to perform day-to-day tasks. ASC provides support based on the need of the resident. Those that live in care homes typically receive a higher level of support, at higher cost, than those that live in the community. Residents can move between care types based on their needs. Understanding these transitions will inform resource planning and help design interventions to maximise the time that people can live in their own homes. 

The aim of the project is to model user transitions between different ASC packages. We want to know what characteristics influence service users' transitions by looking at the long-term journey of an individual and how likely they are to go from one type of care to another.

We applied a multi-state model to data from adults receiving a local authority social care package between 2020 and 2024.  We estimated the probability of transitions across three states: Community-based, Care home, and End-of-life. This approach allowed us to quantify user journeys over time and identify factors related to transitions.

From the transition probability matrix at 1 year, people receiving community-based care had a 3% probability of moving into a Care home. This increased to 12% at year 5. Differences by gender were seen, with men in a Care home having a 30% probability of moving into Community based care versus 13% for women at year 5.

The Model will forecast the number of care home places that will be needed over the next 10 years. Findings are being discussed with stakeholders to consider what targeted initiatives could be tested to lower the probability of transition into a care home. 

The model could be extended by adding another state for people not receiving ASC."


Mai Stafford (Brent Council)
Adshayan Saravanamuthu, (Brent Council)

videos.title: HACA2025- Day 2 - Improving System Flow
videos.description:
Evolving a national diabetes learning health system: Lessons from trials embedded within a national audit

Introduction: 
Some patients do not receive recommended care. For example, there are big differences in how well primary care networks help patients to reduce blood glucose levels and associated risks. To improve care, national organisations provide interventions (e.g. webinars) to clinical teams. It is not known how best to target interventions (e.g. to address higher risks faced by young adults with type 2 diabetes) or whether such interventions lead to improvement or are value-for-money.

Aim & methods:
Through collaboration, we have embedded a cluster randomised controlled trial within the National Diabetes Audit to evaluate interventions it delivers to improve the care and outcomes for people with diabetes. 
Design: Efficient 3-arm cluster randomised trial with process and economic evaluations using routine NDA data.
Participants: All 1283 Primary Care Networks in England
Interventions: Medium-intensity feedback facilitation, delivered through webinars and multi-site calls; Low-intensity feedback facilitation contains similar content delivered through e-learning and email.
Comparator: Usual care (waitlist control group)
Outcomes: Blood glucose of young adults (18-39years) with type 2 diabetes and baseline above NICE-recommended levels. Theory-informed exploration of intervention implementation, engagement fidelity and tailoring. Investigation of cost-effectiveness and budget impact.   

Results & Impact:
This is our second embedded evaluation. Each pragmatic trial gives rigorous information about (cost-)effectiveness to the funders and providers of routinely delivered interventions. Such information enables the national audit to continually improve care and outcomes, and in doing so become a learning health system. 

Lessons learned: 
We endorse calls to move beyond designing and delivering one-off trials and towards sustainable learning health systems that bring together routine data, evaluation capabilities and intervention providers. Such learning health systems can efficiently trial multiple improvement interventions to target inequalities and implementation challenges. We will open a discussion about factors that enable or hinder embedding rigorous evaluations of implementation strategies within healthcare systems.

Michael Sykes, Vice-Chancellor's Fellow C National Audit Improvement Lead (Northumbria University National Diabetes Audit)
Dr Bethan Copsey, Principal Moedical Statistician (University of Leeds)
